html-encoder-decoder.quickAnswer: Encoding turns <div> into <div> so code displays as text instead of rendering. Decoding reverses it. Paste your snippet, pick Encode or Decode, and copy the result - all instantly in your browser.
keyFacts: The five characters that must be escaped in HTML text: & → &, < → <, > → >, " → ", ' → '.
& must be escaped first - escaping it last would double-encode the other entities.
Browsers decode named entities (&), decimal (&) and hex (&) forms.
Encoding user input before inserting it into HTML is the basic defense against XSS attacks.
In code samples and tutorials, unescaped < > would vanish or break the page - encoding keeps them visible.
Decoding is safe: it only translates entities, it never executes scripts.
howTo: Choose the Encode tab to escape HTML, or Decode to reverse entities.
Paste or type your text in the input box.

faqs.q: Why do I need to encode HTML?
faqs.a: Because <, > and & have special meaning in HTML. To show code as visible text - in a tutorial, comment, or CMS - you must escape them, or the browser will try to render them as markup and your text will vanish or break the layout.

faqs.q: What is the difference between < and < ?
faqs.a: They look identical when rendered, but in source code < is the four-character entity that displays as <. Raw < starts a tag. Encoding converts the raw character into the safe entity form.

Encoding user text before inserting it into HTML is the foundation of XSS defense - injected <script> becomes harmless visible text. But full protection also needs context-aware escaping (attributes, JS, URLs) and ideally a sanitizer for rich HTML.
Because the other replacements introduce & characters (< contains &). If & were escaped last, < would become &lt; - double-encoded garbage. Order matters.
Entities written as numbers: & (decimal) or & (hex) both mean &. They work for any Unicode character, e.g. 😀 for an emoji, without needing a named entity.
Yes - decoding only translates entity text back to characters. It does not execute anything. The result is plain text in the output box, never rendered as live HTML.

mistakes: Encoding twice turns < into &lt; — visible garbage. If entities show up as literal text on your page, you encoded an already-encoded string.
Encoding the whole HTML page instead of just the text snippet breaks every tag — encode only the content that must display as text.
Decoding does not make text safe — it's just translation. Pasting decoded output into innerHTML re-arms any script it contained.
& must be escaped first; escaping it last double-encodes everything (< becomes &lt;). Order is the whole trick.
Encoding once and assuming XSS is solved — context matters. Attribute and JavaScript contexts need their own escaping on top of this.
